Dermatology · published research

Acrodermatitis continua

One case report describes marked improvement after polarized light was added for refractory acrodermatitis continua. It cannot establish that light caused the change.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One case report describes marked improvement after polarized light was added for refractory acrodermatitis continua. It cannot establish that light caused the change.

Summary of the Evidence

One direct publication is available: a case report of a pregnant woman with refractory acrodermatitis continua. It has no control group or independent replication. The report concerns one patient and one broad-spectrum polarized light device, so it does not establish effects for other PBM devices or for the wider group of pustular skin disorders.

Human and clinical evidence

The case describes substantial improvement after previous treatment with a potent topical corticosteroid had not controlled the lesions. The patient received polarized, polychromatic noncoherent light, with improvement reported after four sessions and maintained during the reported follow-up. The authors described no treatment-related adverse effect. As a single case, the report cannot distinguish the contribution of light from natural fluctuation, stopping or changing other treatment, or other concurrent care (Choi et al. 2011).

Animal evidence

No animal study specific to acrodermatitis continua was identified in the mapped category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No indication-specific cell, tissue, or mechanistic study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reported exposure used polarized broadband light at a fluence of 10 J/cm², delivered once or twice weekly. The light was polychromatic rather than one narrow wavelength, so it should not be described simply as a red or near-infrared laser protocol. The publication does not establish an optimal schedule or compare alternative wavelengths or doses. A single pregnancy case also cannot define safety across pregnancy or other patient groups.

Interpretation

The report records improvement in one patient after a light-based treatment was introduced. It is a clinical observation, not a controlled estimate of efficacy or safety. Replication and prospective comparison would be needed to determine whether the treatment contributed to the outcome.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for improvement in acrodermatitis continua
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The evidence is one uncontrolled case report in a pregnant patient. The reported improvement is worth recording, but natural fluctuation and concurrent care cannot be separated from the light treatment. Repeated case documentation with complete dosing details, followed by a prospective comparison, would be needed before estimating how often patients benefit.
